title: Universal Dynamics of a Spin-$3/2$ Fermi Gas in Traps with Distinct Spectra
abstract: Universal power-law decay of spin-mixing oscillations has been observed in a harmonically trapped spin-$3/2$ Fermi gas, whose exactly equally spaced spectrum represents a highly special case. To gain insight into the origin of this behavior, we investigate the dynamics in traps with increasing and decreasing level spacings, represented by the infinite square well and the Pöschl--Teller potential, respectively. Despite pronounced differences in their single-particle spectra, all systems exhibit power-law decay of coherent oscillations, described by $A(t) = A_{0} - γt^α$. The exponent $α$ remains insensitive to particle number, interaction strength, and the overall energy scale, but exhibits systematic differences among traps with distinct spectral structures. In contrast, the decay parameter $γ$ is strongly influenced by both the spectral structure and the overall energy scale. These findings demonstrate that power-law decay is not restricted to the harmonic trap but persists across qualitatively distinct spectral structures. The observed variation of $α$ among different traps further suggests that the underlying single-particle spectrum plays an important role in shaping the decay dynamics.
summary: The authors study spin-mixing dynamics in a spin-3/2 Fermi gas trapped in three different potentials (ISW, HOT, PTP) to test the universality of power-law decay. They find that while the decay exponent ($\alpha$) is dictated by the specific spectral structure, the decay parameter ($\gamma$) is sensitive to interaction strength and trap size. This demonstrates that power-law decay is a robust feature not limited to the harmonic trap.
main_problem: To investigate the origin and robustness of universal power-law decay of spin-mixing oscillations in a spin-3/2 Fermi gas, moving beyond the highly special case of the harmonic trap.
main_result: Power-law decay persists across qualitatively distinct spectral structures (ISW, HOT, PTP), and while the decay exponent ($\alpha$) is robustly determined by the spectral structure, the decay parameter ($\gamma$) is sensitive to the overall energy scale and interaction strength.
method: The dynamics are analyzed using the Time-Dependent Hartree-Fock (TDHF) approximation applied to a spin-3/2 Fermi gas confined in three different 1D potentials.
model_or_system: The system is a spin-3/2 Fermi gas governed by a Hamiltonian including single-particle ($H_0$) and interaction ($H_I$) terms. Three traps are compared: the Infinite Square Well (ISW), the Harmonic Oscillator Trap (HOT), and the Pöschl-Teller Potential (PTP).
key_observables: Coherent spin-mixing oscillations exhibiting power-law decay, characterized by the amplitude decay $A(t) = A_0 - \gamma t^\alpha$.
important_parameters: The decay exponent ($\alpha$) and decay parameter ($\gamma$). The comparison fixes the lowest excitation energy spacing ($\Delta E_1 = 1$) to isolate spectral structure effects.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the TDHF approximation and assumes the weak-interaction regime where interaction energy is smaller than the characteristic single-particle level spacing.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the comparison of $\alpha$ and $\gamma$ across ISW, HOT, and PTP traps, showing systematic differences in $\alpha$ but similar scaling behavior for $\gamma$ when varying trap width.
paper_structure: The paper compares the spin-mixing dynamics in three distinct 1D traps (ISW, HOT, PTP) by analyzing the power-law decay of oscillations. It first establishes the persistence of power-law decay across different spectral structures, then quantifies the dependence of the decay exponent ($\alpha$) and parameter ($\gamma$) on spectral geometry and interaction strength.
why_interesting: This work provides a general understanding of how spectral geometry dictates non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body quantum systems, suggesting that the underlying single-particle spectrum is a key determinant of relaxation rates, which is highly relevant for understanding decoherence in quantum simulators.
